title: News, Spelling and Print Around the World
summary: The first newspaper appeared in Strasbourg in 1605, and soon people everywhere could read the news every week or even every day. Young Benjamin Franklin printed a famous almanac, Samuel Johnson wrote a giant dictionary, and a new law gave authors the right to own their books. Printing presses also sailed across oceans to Mexico, India, Massachusetts and Istanbul.

sections.heading: Strasbourg, 1605: The Birth of the Newspaper
paragraphs: How did people get news before newspapers? For most of history the answer was by word of mouth: travellers, merchants, soldiers and pilgrims carried stories from place to place, and town criers shouted announcements in the square. Rich merchants and rulers had something better. They paid for private, handwritten newsletters, sent regularly by post from busy trading cities. In Venice these handwritten news sheets were called avvisi, meaning notices. They reported battles, prices, shipwrecks, royal weddings and the arrival of ships, because for a merchant, knowing the news first could mean making or losing a fortune.

In the 1500s printers also sold one-off news pamphlets about especially exciting events, such as a great battle, a comet or a terrible flood. But these appeared only when something dramatic happened. A newspaper is different: it comes out regularly, on a schedule, with a mix of the latest news, and readers come back for the next issue.

Our first clear example comes from Strasbourg, then a German-speaking free city on the river Rhine, the same city where Gutenberg had done his secret experiments about 170 years earlier. There a bookseller named Johann Carolus had been making money by producing handwritten weekly news reports for paying customers. Copying them out by hand was slow. So Carolus bought a printing workshop, which had belonged to a printer named Thomas Jobin who had died, and installed it in his own house. Then he started printing his weekly news instead of copying it.

We know this because of a letter. In December 1605 Carolus sent a petition to the Strasbourg city council asking for protection against rivals who might copy his idea. In it he explained that he had already been printing his weekly news for some time. This petition was rediscovered in the Strasbourg city archive in the 1980s, and historians now treat it as the newspaper's birth certificate. The earliest issues that still survive date from 1609, and a volume of that year has been digitized by Heidelberg University Library, so anyone can read it online.

Carolus called his paper the Relation, short for a long German title meaning Account of all distinguished and memorable news. In 2005 the World Association of Newspapers accepted the evidence and recognized the Relation of 1605 as the world's first newspaper. Some scholars argue about definitions, because the Relation looked like a little book rather than a big folded sheet, but it was printed, it was regular and it was full of current news, so most people accept its claim.

sections.heading: Corantos, Gazettes and the First Daily
paragraphs: Once the idea existed, it spread quickly. A weekly paper called the Aviso was printed in Wolfenbüttel in northern Germany by 1609. Amsterdam, a busy trading port full of printers, became a great news center. From 1618 Dutch printers produced single-sheet news reports called corantos, meaning currents of news. In 1620 the first news sheets in English were actually printed in Amsterdam and shipped across the North Sea to London, because English printers were tightly controlled at home.

Early newspapers were careful. Kings did not like criticism, so papers mostly reported foreign news, which was safer than writing about your own government. Some papers were official. In England the London Gazette, first published in 1665 as the Oxford Gazette while the royal court had moved to Oxford to escape the plague, printed government announcements, and it still exists today.

Things changed when England's Licensing Act, which had required printed works to be approved in advance, was allowed to lapse in 1695. Suddenly many new papers appeared in London. On 11 March 1702 came the Daily Courant, the first daily newspaper in English. It was started by Elizabeth Mallet, who printed it near the King's Arms tavern at Fleet Bridge in London. Yes, the first English daily was launched by a woman, at a time when very few women ran businesses openly.

The Daily Courant was tiny by modern standards: a single printed sheet, with news on the front and advertisements on the back. Mallet promised readers something interesting. She said she would report only the news, mostly translated from foreign papers, and add no comments of her own, trusting readers to make up their own minds. After about forty days she sold the paper to Samuel Buckley, who ran it for many years. It lasted until 1735, when it merged with another paper.

Across the Atlantic, the first attempt at a newspaper in the English colonies, Publick Occurrences in Boston in 1690, was shut down by the government after just one issue. The Boston News-Letter, begun in 1704, lasted much longer. Newspapers, coffee houses and postal services grew together. In London, people gathered in coffee houses to read the papers aloud and argue about them, so one copy might have many readers. By the 1700s the newspaper had become part of everyday life in many European and colonial cities.

sections.heading: Ballads, Almanacs and Benjamin Franklin's Print Shop
paragraphs: Newspapers were not the only cheap print. Imagine walking through a busy market town in England around 1650. Pasted on walls and posts you might see broadsides: big single sheets printed on one side, used for royal proclamations, notices of executions, advertisements, warnings and news of wonders like a two-headed calf. A seller might be singing ballads, songs printed on cheap sheets with a woodcut picture at the top, telling stories of love, murder, shipwrecks and battles. For a penny you could buy one and learn the words.

Travelling sellers called chapmen walked from village to village with packs full of chapbooks, small cheap booklets of folk tales, jokes, riddles, adventure stories and advice. For many families, chapbooks and ballads were the first things they ever owned in print. These humble products were not considered great literature, but they helped millions of ordinary people get used to reading.

The best-selling printed item of all in many homes was the almanac, a yearly booklet with a calendar, the dates of fairs and holidays, times of sunrise and sunset, phases of the Moon, tides, weather predictions, astrology, recipes and advice. Farmers used almanacs to plan planting, and many families hung one by the fireplace all year.

No one shows the life of a printer in this period better than Benjamin Franklin. He was born in Boston in 1706, the fifteenth of seventeen children of a candle and soap maker. When Ben was twelve, his father apprenticed him to his older brother James, a printer. In 1721 James started a newspaper, the New-England Courant. Ben, then about sixteen, wanted to write for it but knew his brother would refuse. So he invented a character, a talkative widow named Silence Dogood, and slipped her letters under the print shop door at night. The letters were printed in 1722 and became popular before Ben admitted he had written them.

The brothers quarrelled, and in 1723 Ben ran away to Philadelphia with almost no money. He worked for other printers, travelled to London to learn more of the trade, and eventually opened his own shop. In 1729 he took over a newspaper, the Pennsylvania Gazette. In December 1732 he published the first Poor Richard's Almanack, for the year 1733, pretending it was written by a poor stargazer called Richard Saunders. He made it funny from the start, predicting the death of a real rival almanac maker, Titan Leeds, so that readers bought the next issue to see what happened.

Poor Richard was a huge success, selling about 10,000 copies a year, an enormous number for the colonies. Readers loved its short sayings, such as early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy and wise. Franklin admitted he collected many of these sayings from older books and polished them. He published the almanac every year until 1758, when he gathered the best proverbs into an essay later called The Way to Wealth, which was reprinted many times.

Franklin's printing business made him wealthy enough to retire from daily printing in 1748, aged about 42, and spend his time on science and public life. He experimented with electricity, helped found a library and a university, and later helped write the Declaration of Independence. Yet he always remembered his trade. As a young man he wrote a joking epitaph for himself beginning The Body of B. Franklin, Printer, and in his will, written in 1788, he described himself first of all as a printer.

sections.heading: Fixing the Words: Spelling and Dictionaries
paragraphs: If you could read a letter written in English in the year 1500, you would be surprised by the spelling. The same writer might spell the same word two or three different ways on one page. There were no rules to break, because there were no official rules. Spelling simply followed how a word sounded to the writer, and English was spoken very differently in different regions. Even William Shakespeare's name was spelled in several different ways during his lifetime, including in his own signatures.

Printing slowly pushed spelling toward one standard. A busy print shop could not keep stopping to decide how to spell each word, so printers developed house habits, and readers who saw thousands of printed pages got used to seeing words spelled in particular ways. London, where most English printing happened, had a strong influence. Spelling did not settle overnight, though. Early compositors sometimes changed spellings to make a line fit, adding or dropping a letter while justifying the line, and printed spelling took more than two centuries to become fairly consistent.

Dictionaries helped fix the words in place. The first English dictionary that explained words in English, Robert Cawdrey's Table Alphabeticall of 1604, listed only about 2,500 hard words. In France, the French Academy, founded in 1635, worked for decades on an official dictionary of the French language, publishing its first edition in 1694.

England had no academy to do this job, so in 1746 a group of London booksellers hired one remarkable, hard-working writer instead: Samuel Johnson. They agreed to pay him 1,500 guineas, a large sum, though he had to pay his helpers out of it. Working in his house in Gough Square in London with a few clerks to copy out quotations, Johnson read widely through English literature, marking passages that showed how words were really used.

His Dictionary of the English Language was published on 15 April 1755, in two huge folio volumes. It defined 42,773 words and included about 114,000 quotations from roughly 500 authors, including Shakespeare and Milton, to show each word in action. Johnson also had a sense of humour. He defined a lexicographer, a person who writes dictionaries, as a harmless drudge, meaning a hard-working but harmless plodder.

Johnson's Dictionary was expensive, but it became the standard English dictionary for well over a century, until the Oxford English Dictionary was published much later. It did not single-handedly decide English spelling, but it greatly strengthened the idea that there was a correct way to spell and use a word, and later dictionaries built on its spellings and definitions.

All this happened as more people learned to read. Literacy is hard to measure for the past, but one clue is how many people could sign their name on documents such as marriage records. In England, historians estimate that by around 1750 roughly 60 percent of men and perhaps 40 percent of women could sign their names, much higher than two centuries before. Cheap print, schools, religion and trade all encouraged reading, and the more people read, the more printers printed.

sections.heading: Who Owns a Book? The Birth of Copyright
paragraphs: Here is a puzzle that printing created. If you write a book and a printer publishes it, can another printer simply copy it and sell cheaper copies? Before printing, this hardly mattered, because copying a book by hand took so long. After printing, it became a big question, because a rival could reset a popular book and undercut the original in a few weeks.

The first answer was the privilege. Governments granted a particular printer the sole right to print a certain book for a few years. Venice gave one of the earliest in 1469, to the printer Johann of Speyer. In England, the Stationers' Company kept a register of who owned the right to print which book. Notice that these rights belonged to printers and booksellers, not to authors. A writer usually sold a manuscript once for a fee and had no further say.

England's licensing system ended in 1695, and the booksellers lobbied Parliament for new protection. The result was a law usually called the Statute of Anne, after Queen Anne. Its official name began An Act for the Encouragement of Learning, which tells you its purpose. It received royal assent on 5 April 1710 and came into force on 10 April 1710.

The Statute of Anne did two revolutionary things. First, it gave the right to copy a book to its author, who could then sell that right to a publisher. Second, the right lasted only for a limited time: 14 years from publication, which could be renewed for a second 14 years if the author was still alive. Books already in print got 21 years. After that, anyone could print the book. Copies made illegally could be destroyed, and those who made them could be fined.

That time limit was a deliberate balance. Authors and publishers got a reward for their work, which encouraged them to write and publish, while the public eventually got the work for free, so that knowledge would spread. Today we call works that nobody owns any more the public domain. Booksellers later argued that copyright should last forever, but in 1774 the House of Lords, in a case called Donaldson v Becket, ruled that it could not.

The Statute of Anne became a model for copyright laws around the world. The first United States copyright law, in 1790, used the very same scheme of 14 years plus a possible 14-year renewal. Copyright terms are much longer today, but the basic idea that creators should own their work for a limited time began in 1710.

sections.heading: Printing Crosses the Oceans
paragraphs: While Europeans argued about news and copyright, printing presses were travelling across the world on ships, mostly carried by missionaries, colonial governments and merchants. This spread was tied up with colonization and conversion, and the people who already lived in these lands did not ask for it. But it also produced the first printed books in many languages, some of which still survive.

The first press in the Americas came to Mexico City, the capital of the Spanish colony of New Spain. A printer from Seville named Juan Cromberger, who never crossed the ocean himself, sent an Italian-born employee named Juan Pablos, originally Giovanni Paoli from near Brescia. Pablos sailed from Seville in June 1539 and reached Mexico City that October. His first book, printed in 1539, was a short guide to Christian teaching in Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, and Spanish. Sadly no copy survives. Pablos printed at least 37 titles before his death around 1560, including in 1555 a Spanish and Nahuatl dictionary by Alonso de Molina, the first dictionary printed in the Americas. The building where he worked in Mexico City is now a museum.

Printing came next to Lima, in Peru, in 1584. Meanwhile, Asia received European-style presses too. In 1556 a ship carrying a press and Jesuit missionaries to Ethiopia stopped at Goa, the Portuguese colony on India's west coast. When the Ethiopian emperor no longer wanted the missionaries, the press stayed in Goa at the Jesuit College of St Paul, run by a Spanish Jesuit printer, João de Bustamante, with an Indian assistant. In 1578 a book in Tamil, printed with Tamil letters, was produced at Quilon in southern India, one of the first books printed in an Indian script.

Jesuits brought a press to Japan in 1590 and printed books in both Latin letters and Japanese. In Manila, in the Philippines, a Christian teaching book called the Doctrina Christiana was printed in 1593, using woodblocks, in Spanish and Tagalog. In China and Korea, where woodblock printing was already centuries old, the European press made little difference for a long time: the old methods worked well and were deeply rooted.

In North America, the English Puritan colony of Massachusetts got its first press in the late 1630s. A minister named Jose Glover bought a press in England and set sail with his family and a locksmith named Stephen Daye, who had agreed to run it. Glover died during the voyage, so the press belonged to his widow, Elizabeth Glover. Daye set up the press in Cambridge, Massachusetts, near the new Harvard College, with his son Matthew, who probably did much of the actual printing.

Their most famous book, printed in 1640, was The Whole Booke of Psalmes, known today as the Bay Psalm Book. It was a new translation of the Psalms into English verse for singing in church, made by local ministers. It was the first book printed in British North America. About 1,700 copies were printed, but only 11 are known today, and only five are complete. In 2013 one sold at auction for 14.2 million US dollars, a record at that time for a printed book.

The Cambridge press later printed something even more remarkable: in 1663 the whole Bible translated into Massachusett, the language of the Native people of the region, by the missionary John Eliot with Native helpers. It was the first complete Bible printed in the Americas, and it was not in English but in an Indigenous language.

sections.heading: Istanbul's Printing Pioneer
paragraphs: The Ottoman Empire was one of the largest and most powerful states in the world, stretching from Hungary across Turkey and the Middle East to North Africa. Its capital, Istanbul, was a great city of scholars, libraries and book markets. People sometimes say that printing was completely banned there for centuries, but the real story is more interesting.

Printing actually arrived in Istanbul quite early, through the empire's religious minorities. Jewish refugees who had been expelled from Spain set up a Hebrew press in Istanbul around 1493, or by 1504 at the latest; historians still debate the exact date. An Armenian printer, Abgar Tokhatetsi, printed books in Armenian in Istanbul in 1567, and a Greek press operated there in 1627. These communities printed books in their own languages and scripts.

For books in Ottoman Turkish and Arabic, however, the hand-copied manuscript remained king for much longer. There were several reasons, and historians still weigh them up. Thousands of skilled scribes and calligraphers earned their living copying books. Beautiful handwriting was deeply admired, and Arabic script, with letters that change shape and join up, was harder to set in metal type than the Latin alphabet. Many people also felt that holy texts, especially the Quran, should be copied by hand with great care and respect.

The man who brought Ottoman Turkish printing into being was İbrahim Müteferrika, born around 1674 in Kolozsvár, today Cluj-Napoca in Romania. He was a Hungarian who came to Istanbul as a young man, became a Muslim and rose to serve the Ottoman government as a diplomat and scholar. In 1726 he wrote an essay explaining the benefits of printing, arguing that it would make books cheaper, more accurate and more widely available, and help the empire keep up with Europe.

He gained support from powerful officials, a religious ruling approving printing for non-religious books, and permission from Sultan Ahmed III in 1727. He worked with Said Efendi, whose father had been the Ottoman ambassador in Paris. Religious books were left out, partly to reassure the scribes and scholars.

Müteferrika's press printed its first book in 1729: a big Arabic-to-Turkish dictionary known as the Vankulu dictionary, in two volumes. Over the next years he printed history books, a grammar, works on geography and the magnetic compass, and Katip Çelebi's world geography, the Cihannüma, with printed maps. By 1743 the press had printed 17 titles (some historians count 16, because two were often bound together).

That might sound small compared with Europe, but it was a real beginning, and it proved that Ottoman Turkish could be printed beautifully with Arabic letters. Printing in the Ottoman world grew much more widely in the 1800s, and today a statue of İbrahim Müteferrika stands near the old book market beside Istanbul's Grand Bazaar.

By the 1700s, then, printing had become a global technology. Presses worked in Mexico City and Lima, Goa and Manila, Cambridge and Philadelphia, Strasbourg and Istanbul. Newspapers brought weekly and even daily news, almanacs sat by fireplaces, dictionaries steadied spelling, and new laws protected authors. Yet the press itself, a wooden frame with a screw pulled by human arms, was not very different from Gutenberg's. That was about to change.

deepDive: What counts as the 'first newspaper' depends on your definition. Media historians usually require four things: mechanical reproduction (printing), regular publication, a general public that can buy it, and a mix of current news. Handwritten Venetian avvisi had regularity but no printing; earlier one-off news pamphlets had printing but no regularity. Johann Carolus's Relation is the earliest known publication to meet all four tests, but the 1605 date rests entirely on his December 1605 petition, since the oldest surviving issues are from 1609. The format argument matters too: the Relation looked like a small quarto booklet, so the typographer Stanley Morison classed it as a 'newsbook' rather than a newspaper. The World Association of Newspapers nonetheless accepted it as the first newspaper in 2005. Copyright raises another long debate. The Statute of Anne (1710) is often called the first modern copyright law, but historians note it was pushed for mainly by London booksellers who had lost their monopoly when licensing lapsed in 1695. Its limited terms (14 years, renewable once by a living author; 21 years for existing books) led to decades of court fights over whether a 'common-law' perpetual copyright also existed, settled against perpetual rights by the House of Lords in Donaldson v Becket (1774). The global spread of the press also deserves careful framing. In Mexico, Goa, Manila and Massachusetts, presses arrived with missionaries and colonial governments, and their first books were mostly religious texts aimed at converting local peoples, yet they also preserved early printed forms of Nahuatl, Tamil, Tagalog and Massachusett. For the Ottoman Empire, older accounts claiming a strict 'ban' on printing are now questioned; historians stress economic factors (a large scribal profession), aesthetic and technical difficulties of Arabic-script type, and the respect owed to hand-copied religious texts. Müteferrika's 17 titles were small in number but showed the technology could work in Ottoman Turkish.
funFact: The first daily newspaper in English, the Daily Courant of 1702, was launched by a woman, Elizabeth Mallet, who promised to print only the facts and leave readers to make up their own minds.
